{:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "530f5767-4f31-5ef7-a6dd-bdeac420a724" :question/math-academy-id "q-94891" :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨t-1,3,2t⟩$ at the point $t=0.$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})),\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t-1,$ $y=3$ and $z=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{2(t-1)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}},\frac{2(3)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}},\frac{2(2t)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),2t⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}⟩\cdot ⟨1,0,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 1+\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 0+\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2t-2+8t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10} \\  & =\frac{10t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(0))] & =\frac{10(0)-2}{5(0)^{2}-2(0)+10} \\  & =\frac{-2}{10} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2989f12e-e4d2-5eea-a076-313f05f3b144" :step/next {:db/id 17592186485633}} {:db/id 17592186485611 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360524 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "336ae663-8acc-530e-96cc-0c9939efc8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2-3{e}^{-1}" :db/id 17592186358206} {:answer/id #uuid "4e8323a2-f87f-54c1-ba41-37494660f68d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3e+{e}^{-1}" :db/id 17592186358429} {:answer/id #uuid "68b9473e-f106-5375-ac81-7275f6b0a9eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{2}-2{e}^{-2}" :db/id 17592186358670} {:answer/id #uuid "734c0594-8b9d-5fed-bb61-015770db6c72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{e}^{2}" :db/id 17592186358754} {:answer/id #uuid "f34de6af-084c-5ec3-8d75-77cbd5aa09e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4{e}^{-1}" :db/id 17592186359914}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186358670} :answer-field/id #uuid "7e56fa10-b537-572f-8386-98aeb21d532f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360205}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "97fd3ba8-8ab5-5d07-adaa-98357dd8d4e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-94873" :question/problem "Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=1$ given that $∇f(x,y)=2x\,i+2y\,j$ and $r(t)={e}^{-t}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=2x\,i+2y\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x={e}^{-t}$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2{e}^{-t}\,i+2{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =(-{e}^{-t})\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2{e}^{-t}\,i+2{e}^{t}\,j)\cdot ((-{e}^{-t})\,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =2{e}^{-t}\cdot (-{e}^{-t})+2{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =2{e}^{2(1)}-2{e}^{-2(1)} \\  & =2{e}^{2}-2{e}^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3232ec86-62d5-5c61-ba3f-93622480e150" :step/next {:db/id 17592186485608}} {:db/id 17592186485628 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360579 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5305687e-83d8-5c87-af7d-a5b0a362d788" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{csc}⁡t+{e}^{{t}^{2}}+t" :db/id 17592186358466} {:answer/id #uuid "631de459-4352-5ad1-949e-8ac23d4b20f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{csc}⁡t+2t{e}^{{t}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186358613} {:answer/id #uuid "b15809fa-40bc-5563-9a51-d40e84efc938" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cot}⁡t+2t{e}^{{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{t}" :db/id 17592186359292} {:answer/id #uuid "c66b80bb-3662-52ab-bf2e-dab3fb4673d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cot}⁡t+{e}^{{t}^{2}}-1" :db/id 17592186359496} {:answer/id #uuid "e0073e63-c4b1-5f0a-b806-ed90e183c49f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{tan}⁡t+\frac{{e}^{{t}^{2}}}{{t}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186359718}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359292} :answer-field/id #uuid "d86a4006-7e81-5ee9-a91c-4ead86d71714" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360371}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "312e3468-92a5-5996-9fc8-ac654be83975" :question/math-academy-id "q-95149" :question/problem "If $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xz)+{e}^{y}$ and $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j+\frac{1}{t}\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xz)+{e}^{y})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xz)+{e}^{y})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xz)+{e}^{y})\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+{e}^{y}\,j+\frac{1}{z}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,y={t}^{2},$ and $z=\frac{1}{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{{t}^{2}}\,j+t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2t\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{{t}^{2}}\,j+t\,k)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2t\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}+2t{e}^{{t}^{2}}-\frac{t}{{t}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡t+2t{e}^{{t}^{2}}-\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a35955fa-8e05-5fc2-9647-6f1fbb5eff50"} {:db/id 17592186485631 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323880 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b203b6e-7830-50da-aa18-f454f862a948" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186321238} {:answer/id #uuid "2cf6d8fc-e1b8-5fdc-b9b5-09f8f6941c20" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi +2}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186321497} {:answer/id #uuid "c175b73f-e2fb-54e8-a7e0-b2906ff65bfd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi +1}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186322651} {:answer/id #uuid "c8d08b91-916d-5adb-a62d-964ea2cc4e5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{\pi +2}" :db/id 17592186322710} {:answer/id #uuid "e1542b36-0e72-5814-8c1f-4765946bc3e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{\pi +1}" :db/id 17592186322908}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186321497} :answer-field/id #uuid "276fef95-8127-5751-a8f3-63d27774306c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323248}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fdba027b-12bc-5b22-aa20-f040a6af0b36" :question/math-academy-id "q-37106" :question/problem "Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=1$ given that $∇f(x,y)=\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j$ and $r(t)=(2{t}^{2}+2)\,i+\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,j.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=2{t}^{2}+2$ and $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}+2}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡t}\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡t)\,j \\  & =4t\,i+\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}+2}\,i+\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (4t\,i+\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}+2}\cdot 4t+\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡t}\cdot \frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+1}+\frac{1}{({t}^{2}+1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{2t\operatorname{arctan}⁡t+1}{({t}^{2}+1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\frac{2(1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+1}{({1}^{2}+1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡1} \\  & =\frac{(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+1)}{(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{\pi +2}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bb7a2b36-6b63-51f3-9376-761d5f709c35" :step/next {:db/id 17592186485611}} {:db/id 17592186485633 :step/content {:db/id 17592186485588 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "131e1312-3232-541a-a772-9a4195876e08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186484854} {:answer/id #uuid "1cf61e8f-1cbe-5cf7-b7de-cb285c2945df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(t+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186484868} {:answer/id #uuid "54a8785f-b684-5fbf-ab5e-7a2651308e2f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186485006} {:answer/id #uuid "7b1155ed-ffcf-5482-9835-4e132b93d976" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186485086} {:answer/id #uuid "7d4e5d76-01d4-5027-9d0b-5f4455a3c94c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186485089}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186485006} :answer-field/id #uuid "26f9db34-f1fa-54a6-9839-7f297b6a756c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186485384}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "eabe5e6a-dc85-5118-84d2-9aa9f31a6a23" :question/math-academy-id "q-95086" :question/problem "If $f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z)$ and $r(t)=(t+1)\,i+2t\,j+{t}^{2}\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z)\,i+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)\,j+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t+1,$ $y=2t$ and $z={t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,j+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,k \\  & =\,i+2\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,j+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,k)\cdot (\,i+2\,j+2t\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\cdot 2+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\cdot 2t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2t(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)(1+t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bd21bb0d-0ac3-5b0d-8a0d-e84c7b42e305" :step/next {:db/id 17592186485628}}] :activity/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule in Vector Form" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186484804} {:db/id 17592186046659} {:db/id 17592186485631 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323880 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b203b6e-7830-50da-aa18-f454f862a948" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186321238} {:answer/id #uuid "2cf6d8fc-e1b8-5fdc-b9b5-09f8f6941c20" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi +2}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186321497} {:answer/id #uuid "c175b73f-e2fb-54e8-a7e0-b2906ff65bfd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi +1}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186322651} {:answer/id #uuid "c8d08b91-916d-5adb-a62d-964ea2cc4e5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{\pi +2}" :db/id 17592186322710} {:answer/id #uuid "e1542b36-0e72-5814-8c1f-4765946bc3e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{\pi +1}" :db/id 17592186322908}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186321497} :answer-field/id #uuid "276fef95-8127-5751-a8f3-63d27774306c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323248}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fdba027b-12bc-5b22-aa20-f040a6af0b36" :question/math-academy-id "q-37106" :question/problem "Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=1$ given that $∇f(x,y)=\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j$ and $r(t)=(2{t}^{2}+2)\,i+\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,j.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=2{t}^{2}+2$ and $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}+2}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡t}\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡t)\,j \\  & =4t\,i+\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}+2}\,i+\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (4t\,i+\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}+2}\cdot 4t+\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡t}\cdot \frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+1}+\frac{1}{({t}^{2}+1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{2t\operatorname{arctan}⁡t+1}{({t}^{2}+1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\frac{2(1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+1}{({1}^{2}+1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡1} \\  & =\frac{(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+1)}{(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{\pi +2}{\pi }.\end{aligned}

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})),\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t-1,$ $y=3$ and $z=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{2(t-1)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}},\frac{2(3)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}},\frac{2(2t)}{(t-1)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2t)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),2t⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10},\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}⟩\cdot ⟨1,0,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{2t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 1+\frac{6}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 0+\frac{4t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2t-2+8t}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10} \\  & =\frac{10t-2}{5{t}^{2}-2t+10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(0))] & =\frac{10(0)-2}{5(0)^{2}-2(0)+10} \\  & =\frac{-2}{10} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2989f12e-e4d2-5eea-a076-313f05f3b144" :step/next {:db/id 17592186485633}} {:db/id 17592186485633 :step/content {:db/id 17592186485588 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "131e1312-3232-541a-a772-9a4195876e08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186484854} {:answer/id #uuid "1cf61e8f-1cbe-5cf7-b7de-cb285c2945df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(t+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186484868} {:answer/id #uuid "54a8785f-b684-5fbf-ab5e-7a2651308e2f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186485006} {:answer/id #uuid "7b1155ed-ffcf-5482-9835-4e132b93d976" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186485086} {:answer/id #uuid "7d4e5d76-01d4-5027-9d0b-5f4455a3c94c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186485089}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186485006} :answer-field/id #uuid "26f9db34-f1fa-54a6-9839-7f297b6a756c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186485384}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "eabe5e6a-dc85-5118-84d2-9aa9f31a6a23" :question/math-academy-id "q-95086" :question/problem "If $f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z)$ and $r(t)=(t+1)\,i+2t\,j+{t}^{2}\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z)\,i+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)\,j+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t+1,$ $y=2t$ and $z={t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,j+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,k \\  & =\,i+2\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,j+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,k)\cdot (\,i+2\,j+2t\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\cdot 2+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\cdot 2t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2t(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)(1+t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bd21bb0d-0ac3-5b0d-8a0d-e84c7b42e305" :step/next {:db/id 17592186485628}} {:db/id 17592186485611 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360524 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "336ae663-8acc-530e-96cc-0c9939efc8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2-3{e}^{-1}" :db/id 17592186358206} {:answer/id #uuid "4e8323a2-f87f-54c1-ba41-37494660f68d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3e+{e}^{-1}" :db/id 17592186358429} {:answer/id #uuid "68b9473e-f106-5375-ac81-7275f6b0a9eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{2}-2{e}^{-2}" :db/id 17592186358670} {:answer/id #uuid "734c0594-8b9d-5fed-bb61-015770db6c72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{e}^{2}" :db/id 17592186358754} {:answer/id #uuid "f34de6af-084c-5ec3-8d75-77cbd5aa09e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4{e}^{-1}" :db/id 17592186359914}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186358670} :answer-field/id #uuid "7e56fa10-b537-572f-8386-98aeb21d532f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360205}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "97fd3ba8-8ab5-5d07-adaa-98357dd8d4e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-94873" :question/problem "Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=1$ given that $∇f(x,y)=2x\,i+2y\,j$ and $r(t)={e}^{-t}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =2{e}^{2(1)}-2{e}^{-2(1)} \\  & =2{e}^{2}-2{e}^{-2}.\end{aligned}

$\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={e}^{t}$ and $y={e}^{-t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2{e}^{t}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t})\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i-{e}^{-t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2{e}^{t}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j)\cdot ({e}^{t}\,i-{e}^{-t}\,j) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{-t} \\  & =2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0cdae9f2-99ba-523d-86fd-08256e29cd00" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515645}} {:db/id 17592186515643 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360547 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "20f3235b-60e2-5c23-a6d1-2912bfc76c91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186358041} {:answer/id #uuid "b7fdac84-5c94-5bcb-847f-c1a99a8c5411" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359347} {:answer/id #uuid "bde855a4-7fc2-52c3-af6f-b2e1fd0d6c05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359405} {:answer/id #uuid "dc8b8503-66f4-52dd-b74c-bee16b502323" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359689} {:answer/id #uuid "e953648a-9a4f-5892-9fbd-2c82540d2fdb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359825}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359405} :answer-field/id #uuid "6b3efa02-f1ae-5df0-98fd-0df55d2c7698" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360170}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "9d03333b-22a3-579a-b479-87085056a6c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-95059" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡xy$ and $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡xy)\,j \\  & =\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,j\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={e}^{t}$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,i+\frac{{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,i+\frac{{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,j)\cdot ({e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}+\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "386e3776-9252-5f0e-9289-19a65b4311b4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515689}} {:db/id 17592186515645 :step/content {:db/id 17592186445680 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4bc8881d-ce79-5fa4-94b3-93194df95932" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{ln}^{2}⁡(\pi )" :db/id 17592186445652} {:answer/id #uuid "76ff76d1-a44d-5785-aeb6-f49cd08b8d01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\pi )" :db/id 17592186445657} {:answer/id #uuid "869d2a2c-eca1-5a81-9c8c-bd38ea652d36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\pi )" :db/id 17592186445658} {:answer/id #uuid "9980bb90-a6ef-51f4-88b3-4812a2e11e8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{ln}^{2}⁡(2\pi )" :db/id 17592186445662} {:answer/id #uuid "e898d08a-c5cb-5c48-be98-c6dd2a755c94" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{ln}^{2}⁡(\pi )" :db/id 17592186445670}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186445652} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6ea0794-709e-5625-aee2-f32cf13014aa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186445676}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b98d6bad-fbc9-5978-8040-a1a35d995f54" :question/math-academy-id "q-36234" :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡t,2t⟩$ at the point $t=\pi .$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{t}+2{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{\pi }+2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3a4200b6-903e-5981-924d-9535282a3f9d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515643}} {:db/id 17592186515689 :step/content {:db/id 17592186515530 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0618c56b-92f8-5743-9e32-328933507a90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}+{t}^{2}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186514887} {:answer/id #uuid "42831ed2-f44c-506e-a16d-0e06ead786c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2t}-{t}^{2}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186515014} {:answer/id #uuid "581a6ccb-d929-5a4c-abd5-314717c764d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2t}+t}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186515068} {:answer/id #uuid "b182ff13-9dbc-5c38-8d5b-05e109460201" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2t}}{\sqrt{{e}^{t}+t}}" :db/id 17592186515243} {:answer/id #uuid "b6bd0e4e-b413-5783-9897-cec63d3177bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{t}^{2}}{\sqrt{{e}^{t}+t}}" :db/id 17592186515258}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186515068} :answer-field/id #uuid "9eb54adf-64fe-5825-9ef0-62336c5f858a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186515471}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2becf284-e142-5ae3-80f6-d208696ea202" :question/math-academy-id "q-95068" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+t\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$

$$

Next, we substitute $x={e}^{t}$ and $y=t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}\,j)\cdot ({e}^{t}\,i+j) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2t}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2t}+t}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+{t}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bf608e7a-0173-58ee-a61e-d120aeb92841" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515711}} {:db/id 17592186515711 :step/content {:db/id 17592186485588 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "131e1312-3232-541a-a772-9a4195876e08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186484854} {:answer/id #uuid "1cf61e8f-1cbe-5cf7-b7de-cb285c2945df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(t+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186484868} {:answer/id #uuid "54a8785f-b684-5fbf-ab5e-7a2651308e2f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186485006} {:answer/id #uuid "7b1155ed-ffcf-5482-9835-4e132b93d976" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186485086} {:answer/id #uuid "7d4e5d76-01d4-5027-9d0b-5f4455a3c94c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})" :db/id 17592186485089}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186485006} :answer-field/id #uuid "26f9db34-f1fa-54a6-9839-7f297b6a756c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186485384}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "eabe5e6a-dc85-5118-84d2-9aa9f31a6a23" :question/math-academy-id "q-95086" :question/problem "If $f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z)$ and $r(t)=(t+1)\,i+2t\,j+{t}^{2}\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z))\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(y+z)\,i+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)\,j+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y+z)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t+1,$ $y=2t$ and $z={t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,j+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,k \\  & =\,i+2\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,j+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\,k)\cdot (\,i+2\,j+2t\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\cdot 2+(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})\cdot 2t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2t(t+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)(1+t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+{t}^{2})+2(t+1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+{t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "fee8b366-8b24-5d5f-8a6e-56a6d4fdb53d"}] :activity/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule in Vector Form" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186514855} {:db/id 17592186046644 :course/id #uuid "992cac0c-bf6a-5373-95c9-02edfcfb591e" :course/math-academy-id 105} {:db/id 17592186515625 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124955 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3d91284b-aa86-5efd-8e00-bc13b952dcba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{2t}+2{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186321627} {:answer/id #uuid "57674ee3-9965-5502-a818-bbcc31f0235a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{e}^{2t}" :db/id 17592186321835} {:answer/id #uuid "60879608-43b6-5c2d-8f50-f7877f002d73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186321904} {:answer/id #uuid "8305ad0c-8f86-50aa-a55a-367d449dabc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{t}-2{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186322180} {:answer/id #uuid "e18c50bc-afa0-58da-b693-f0e3601201ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186322910}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186321904} :answer-field/id #uuid "f71b9994-814b-5c24-af5b-f67cb4ffae0f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323654}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5ea55a51-bc91-526a-9277-7689869bc683" :question/math-academy-id "q-36211" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{-t}\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$

Next, we substitute $x={e}^{t}$ and $y={e}^{-t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

:question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{t}+2{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{\pi }+2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3a4200b6-903e-5981-924d-9535282a3f9d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515643}} {:db/id 17592186515643 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360547 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "20f3235b-60e2-5c23-a6d1-2912bfc76c91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186358041} {:answer/id #uuid "b7fdac84-5c94-5bcb-847f-c1a99a8c5411" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359347} {:answer/id #uuid "bde855a4-7fc2-52c3-af6f-b2e1fd0d6c05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359405} {:answer/id #uuid "dc8b8503-66f4-52dd-b74c-bee16b502323" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359689} {:answer/id #uuid "e953648a-9a4f-5892-9fbd-2c82540d2fdb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{t}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}" :db/id 17592186359825}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359405} :answer-field/id #uuid "6b3efa02-f1ae-5df0-98fd-0df55d2c7698" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360170}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "9d03333b-22a3-579a-b479-87085056a6c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-95059" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡xy$ and $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,i+\frac{{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,j)\cdot ({e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}+\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{1+{e}^{2t}{sin}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{3\cdot (-1)+5\cdot 1+5\cdot (-1)}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{a}_{1}=-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{3\cdot (-3)+5\cdot (-2)+5\cdot 1}{(-3)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =-\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{10\cdot (-2)+6\cdot 1+14\cdot 3}{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}v=2\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{10\cdot 2+6\cdot (-2)+14\cdot 2}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}w=3\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 2 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -6 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

{:db/id 17592186135048 :tutorial/content "If $\big\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \big\}$ is a set of orthogonal vectors, then the **orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$** is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+⋯+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{n}}x \\  & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}+\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}+⋯+\frac{x\cdot {a}_{n}}{{a}_{n}\cdot {a}_{n}}{a}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is the sum of the orthogonal projections of $\mathbf{x}$ onto each one-dimensional subspace of $\textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \big\}.$

**Watch out!** The formula works *only* when the set of vectors $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is orthogonal!

In case of a $2$-dimensional subspace $S=\textrm{Span} \big\{ \mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2 \big\},$ we can visualize the orthogonal projection geometrically, as follows:

$$
{\color{blue}\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x}} 
	= 
	{\color{red}\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}_1}\mathbf{x}} + {\color{red}\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbf{x}}
$$

\mathbf{a}_2.$ 

We start by writing $\mathbf{x}$ as a sum of two vectors

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_S + \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp},
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_S=\text{proj}_S\,\mathbf{x}$ is in $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\},$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ is in the orthogonal complement of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$. That is, $\mathbf{x}_S=k_1\mathbf{a}_1+k_2\mathbf{a}_2\in S\,$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp.$

From the equation above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\  & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\  & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the fact that $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ is orthogonal to $S,$ and the fact that $\mathbf{a}_1\cdot\mathbf{a}_2=0,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{2}=0\end{aligned} & \,\,\,⟹\,\,\,\{\begin{aligned}(x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2})\cdot {a}_{1}=0 \\ (x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2})\cdot {a}_{2}=0\end{aligned} \\  & \,\,\,⟹\,\,\,\{\begin{aligned}x\cdot {a}_{1}-{k}_{1}({a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1})-{k}_{2}({a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{1})=0 \\ x\cdot {a}_{2}-{k}_{1}({a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{2})-{k}_{2}({a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2})=0\end{aligned} \\  & \,\,\,⟹\,\,\,\{\begin{aligned}{k}_{1}({a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1})=x\cdot {a}_{1} \\ {k}_{2}({a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2})=x\cdot {a}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & \,\,\,⟹\,\,\,\{\begin{aligned}{k}_{1}=\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}} \\ {k}_{2}=\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain our formula 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2} \\  & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}+\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "adabdbc0-f726-5b67-81e5-73ef172ea7cf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4345 :tutorial/title "Justification of the Formula"} :step/id #uuid "5dcbfead-f350-544f-a0c0-5ef1f197ee0f" :step/math-academy-id 26425} {:db/id 17592186134769 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135088 :tutorial/content "Let $n,m$ be positive integers such that $n\leq m.$ Given an orthogonal set $\big\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \big\} \subset  \Bbb R^m$ and a vector $\mathbf x \in \Bbb R^m,$ we define the **distance between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the vector space $S=\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,  \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$** as

$$
\Vert{ \color{purple} \mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} }\Vert.
$$

We can also define the **angle between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$** to be the acute angle $\theta$ between the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and its orthogonal projection $\text{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x},$ as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/07/07fa0d011bbfd49f89ddc5035a27839640a0c2624046d39fbfe8f57c476b5b25.png)

 

Finally, notice that we can represent the vector $\mathbf{x}$ as a sum of two orthogonal vectors:

$$
\mathbf{x} = \underbrace{\textrm{proj}_{S}\mathbf{x}}_{\large \in S} + \underbrace{(\mathbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\mathbf{x})}_{\large \in S^\perp}
$$

 

**Note:** The vector $\textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x},$ whose norm $\| \textbf{x}-\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} \|$ represents the distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to $S,$ is sometimes called the **vector rejection of $\mathbf{x}$ from $S.$**" :tutorial/id #uuid "0c1861f6-1be0-5e7e-88be-6186634715ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4346 :tutorial/title "The Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace"} :step/id #uuid "6328b011-7457-5a1a-b13f-1e2b37822525" :step/math-academy-id 26428 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134673}} {:db/id 17592186134773 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133844 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133659 :question/id #uuid "7014f0ec-9ce3-598a-8ddb-b71a000d383f" :question/math-academy-id "e-7309"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c93bf305-85ff-5455-91ba-ae60f3c1989d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050336}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134273} {:db/id 17592186134300} {:db/id 17592186272093} {:db/id 17592186326859} {:db/id 17592186351467} {:db/id 17592186351468} {:db/id 17592186351469} {:db/id 17592186351470} {:db/id 17592186351473} {:db/id 17592186351474} {:db/id 17592186371831} {:db/id 17592186481667}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Acute Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "42dfcb52-37d6-5cd0-9c79-bb0c59437b69" :step/math-academy-id 27054 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134768}}] :activity/title "Projecting Vectors Onto Subspaces in Euclidean Spaces (Orthogonal Bases)" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134002} {:db/id 17592186134672 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135048 :tutorial/content "If $\big\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \big\}$ is a set of orthogonal vectors, then the **orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$** is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+⋯+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{n}}x \\  & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}+\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}+⋯+\frac{x\cdot {a}_{n}}{{a}_{n}\cdot {a}_{n}}{a}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is the sum of the orthogonal projections of $\mathbf{x}$ onto each one-dimensional subspace of $\textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \big\}.$

**Watch out!** The formula works *only* when the set of vectors $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is orthogonal!

In case of a $2$-dimensional subspace $S=\textrm{Span} \big\{ \mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2 \big\},$ we can visualize the orthogonal projection geometrically, as follows:

$$
{\color{blue}\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x}} 
	= 
	{\color{red}\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}_1}\mathbf{x}} + {\color{red}\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbf{x}}
$$

![](images/7d/7d27747451504c7244ddac4609c9c205c60cd525de2cfd364c20e90c1655ef4e.png)

**Note:** A proof of the formula will be provided at the end of the lesson. Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$" :question/worked-solution "Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{(-9)\cdot 4+2\cdot (-4)+31\cdot 2}{{4}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+{2}^{2}}v=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{(-9)\cdot 3+2\cdot 2+31\cdot (-2)}{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}w=-5\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-5\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-15 \\ -10 \\ 10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-13 \\ -12 \\ 11\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "07f5fb55-5a96-560a-81bc-2ee4ef08eb3a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186488328}} {:db/id 17592186488315 :step/content {:db/id 17592186326864 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0368bac0-984e-5787-80ab-57f2797279e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}20 \\ 20 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186324006} {:answer/id #uuid "146ade24-131c-5a2f-b98f-ec8b390c591c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}20 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186324156} {:answer/id #uuid "8957b4dc-3288-5bc8-94b9-4b3ea2e960ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 40 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186325143} {:answer/id #uuid "98e891e2-50be-5dde-9dc9-f9157bf702d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}20 \\ 40 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186325271} {:answer/id #uuid "ab03c3c3-e63d-51f9-b995-161f52c4e24f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}20 \\ -20 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186325426}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186325426} :answer-field/id #uuid "7f98642b-b39d-56b1-9d79-30da4adf0483" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326452}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3e6b99aa-c1fb-5c62-9a05-f09dd90462a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-40616" :question/problem "Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ where

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -4 \\ 0 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 5 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ 5 \\ 0 \\ -8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 6 \\ 0 \\ -17\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,w=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,\,x=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane given that $v⊥w.$" :question/worked-solution "Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{v,w\}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ 
And, since the set $\{v,w\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by 

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}v=\frac{2}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{3\cdot 2+1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}w=\frac{11}{6}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{11}{6}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(4\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+11\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ \frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a4cae37a-e3ec-588f-b8a6-214967984746" :step/next {:db/id 17592186494064}} {:db/id 17592186494047 :step/content {:db/id 17592186351311 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27b82414-74c1-5544-b30e-ddd2ce021c54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186348789} {:answer/id #uuid "4fd8c6cb-3a96-578f-b2a9-ef7282b4d01c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186349168} {:answer/id #uuid "7eadf76b-0b7f-5519-8f83-c78f340e603e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186349607} {:answer/id #uuid "d5d514c7-4c99-5779-b25c-30bbeb2dbecb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186350325} {:answer/id #uuid "e1900fb2-02e4-590c-a21d-1384d20d2199" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186350429}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349607} :answer-field/id #uuid "4df8697c-19ab-5320-a7f6-eea91212521d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350840}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f5a26e7c-2fff-5f64-bdf0-4a1fa47a2fd4" :question/math-academy-id "q-81472" :question/problem "Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,\,x=\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal." :question/worked-solution "Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\},$ $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\},$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{3}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1+4\cdot 0}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{7\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0+4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=3\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{3}}{{a}_{3}\cdot {a}_{3}}{a}_{3}=\frac{7\cdot (-3)+3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 2+4\cdot 2}{(-3)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{3}}x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+3\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+(-1)\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f3b630ff-474b-5c65-b9cb-a6f7547e51ad"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9579ba9f-4993-5923-aa2e-30446e774e93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value ![](images/e3/e3feb58766bbbb4dc2ed0cd738c7a5d74d31a6d3bbc2e210010b9e5ecbc21da8.png)" :question/worked-solution "Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when $f'(x)=0$ or $f'(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there are two critical points:

$$
x=-1\quad \text{and} \quad x=1
$$

Also, we have the following:

- If $f'(x) > 0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.
- If $f'(x) < 0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty)$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $f'$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $f$ | $\nearrow$ | $\textrm{max}$ | $\searrow$ | $\textrm{not extr.}$ | $\searrow$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$:

- First, we draw the critical points. We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical lines $x=-1$ and $x=1$. Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $\searrow$ on $(-1,1)$, the point at $x=1$ must be lower than the point at $x=-1$, as shown below.

![](images/27/27cfed2793c78d0abaa91c4d5480724303ebf729fa22befbd6142e8e54039e64.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:Since $f(x)$ is increasing $\nearrow$ on $(-\infty,-1)$ and decreasing $\searrow$ on $(-1,1)$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes down to the left and the right of $x=-1$. Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $\searrow$ on $(-1,1)$ and decreasing $\searrow$ on $(1,\infty)$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes up to the left and goes down to the right of $x=1$. Furthermore, since $f'(x)$ is increasing to the left of $x = 1$, we must have $f''(x) > 0$, and, since it is decreasing to the right of $x = 1$, we must have $f''(x) < 0$. So, $x =1$ is an inflection point at which the curve $y=f(x)$ changes from concave up to concave down.

![](images/15/15842026cf3d019dcfd31c0f4f9aad54a4c8465dc1464feaa2d07b45e109ef74.png)

- Finally, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,2)$ | $2$ | $(2, \infty)$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $f'$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $\nearrow$ | $\textrm{max}$ | $\searrow$ | $\textrm{min}$ | $\nearrow$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$:

- First, we draw the critical points. Consider the vertical lines $x=1$ and $x=2$. We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical line $x=1$.Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $\searrow$ on $(1,2)$, the point at $x=2$ must be lower than the point at $x=1$.

So, we draw it as follows:

![](images/e3/e3a15ad7af8061bb800c5536fe054594402c7898ef7485a8a4165aff9cdc272d.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:Since $f(x)$ is increasing $\nearrow$ on $(-\infty,1)$ and decreasing $\searrow$ on $(1,2)$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes down to the left and to the right of $x=1$.Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $\searrow$ on $(1,2)$ and increasing $\nearrow$ on $(2,\infty)$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes up to the left and to the right of $x=2$.Furthermore, since $f'(x)$ is increasing to the left of $x = 3$, we must have $f''(x) > 0$. So, the curve $y=f(x)$ is concave up on $(2,3)$. Also, since $f'(x)$ is constant and positive to the right of $x = 3$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ represents a section of an increasing straight line on $(3,\infty)$.

![](images/20/200f45be73f0c38d5cab4099ac83ab5d80022539e17cd0996f1ab0228a90a89e.png)

- Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x)$:

![](images/16/16aff3b702623f3b6339cacfcdac4c9b43900e58f1228481d168b8b0535e1412.png)

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. "16166227-96e3-5281-9560-ed98cac88477" :topic/math-academy-id 1206} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186101610 :step/content {:db/id 17592186102005 :tutorial/content "The graph of $y=f'(x)$, the derivative of $y=f(x)$ is shown below. Let's use this to sketch a possible graph of the original function, $y=f(x)$.

![](images/6c/6cd6c0fa999d571b54b7408856ecc8d091c2f4bb16b9f7bf85eb7f91b05629e4.png)

Recall that the critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when $f'(x)=0$ or $f'(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there are two critical points:

$$
x=-3\quad \textrm{and} \quad x=1
$$

Also, we have the following:

- If $f'(x) > 0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.
- If $f'(x) < 0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty,-3)$ | $-3$ | $(-3,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty)$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $f'$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $\nearrow$ | $\textrm{max}$ | $\searrow$ | $\textrm{min}$ | $\nearrow$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$:

- First, we draw the critical points. We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical lines $x=-3$ and $x=1$. Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $\searrow$ on $(-3,1)$, the point at $x=1$ must be lower than the point at $x=-3$, as shown below.

![](images/cb/cb0de4712344b43d32343f4d9fbc11d3dbc5c96df858f27bee599a3ffdd448ce.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:Since $f(x)$ is increasing $\nearrow$ on $(-\infty,-3)$ and decreasing $\searrow$ on $(-3,1)$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes down to the left and to the right of $x=-3$.Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $\searrow$ on $(-3,1)$ and increasing $\nearrow$ on $(1,\infty)$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes up to the left and to the right of $x=1$.

![](images/34/3498651b6a642f59068f23e8ed9ddd211bfb76ab4d0bf8e28cefd84d1a4b2aed.png)

- Finally, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x)$:

![](images/25/257203aa25e423bf82ce745a6a8a3563aa80e414e9dfadf0be64629624cbce0e.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "0173ff8c-84c4-5761-9aad-f4e4362d1e7f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 651 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7be92f4e-9fd4-54b7-90b1-2736d279c774" :step/math-academy-id 1244 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101612}} {:db/id 17592186101611 :step/content {:db/id 17592186100829 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100640 :question/id #uuid "9b188b17-3d3f-5063-b12b-cdc6b58191d6" :question/math-academy-id "e-339"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4cad1e6a-c137-573e-8cad-c992931540a6" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101308} {:db/id 17592186101310}] :knowledge-point/title "Sketching a Function Given the Graph of its Derivative"} :step/id #uuid "abfe8a46-b88e-5eee-890a-9ec5626d0c97" :step/math-academy-id 1245 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101613}} {:db/id 17592186101612 :step/content {:db/id 17592186102006 :tutorial/content "Let's draw our possible function $y=f(x)$ once more. The graph of its derivative $y=f'(x)$ is also shown.

![](images/18/189c181d3767960f39fc0cfcb06dac5bf6fca07e303b11999307551d081ffc1e.png)

In reality, there are infinitely many possible graphs of $f(x)$ that can be drawn if we are given only the graph of $f'(x)$. We can always shift the graph up and down as we please, because the slopes of the tangent lines do not change. For the problem above, any of the following graphs would be valid:

![](images/e4/e49f65d7306192d73001552084f06cf39731f38f3ccc14dd6b2f5f7641ec43aa.png)

In this topic, we will focus on sketching a *possible* graph of $y=f(x)$ given the graph of $y=f'(x)$. But bear in mind that whatever $y=f(x)$ we sketch, we can get an equally valid answer by shifting or $y=f(x)$ curve up or down by an arbitrary amount.

The only exception is if we're given a point on the curve $y=f(x)$. If we're given a point, this has the effect of *fixing* our answer to a particular curve. We'll see an example of this next." :tutorial/id #uuid "aed3a1d0-c855-5799-a9a4-76d3c17c10bf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 653 :tutorial/title "Non-Uniqueness in Sketching a Function Given the Graph of :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite

$$
\dfrac{1}{8}
$$

as a power of $2$ (the base of the logarithm) as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{1}{2^3} = 2^{-3}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\log_{2} \left(\dfrac 1 {8} \right)= \log_{2} (2^{-3})
$$

Now we can proceed as usual. The log of a power of the base equals the power itself:

$$
\log_b(b^x) = x
$$

In our case, we have $b=2$ and $x=-3$. Therefore,

$$
\log_{2}(2^{-3})= -3
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064708 :question/id #uuid "77b9cc7f-1d13-5090-b38b-20e0a52ec9d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-2946"} {:db/id 17592186064709 :question/id #uuid "42c2d551-1318-51f9-9053-ece7f4a3f0f2" :question/math-academy-id "q-2951"} {:db/id 17592186064192 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064067 :question/id #uuid "d137aa5c-f148-5a6f-bbda-0d88557f8ea9" :question/math-academy-id "e-3987"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cc1c6931-cc04-5014-9bf6-5ebc5dc07728" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064667 :question/id #uuid "efed6494-6266-5ffa-88eb-576a200cbbd2" :question/math-academy-id "q-25790"} {:db/id 17592186064707 :question/id #uuid "234787b2-30f7-59c7-9eef-14e302d5d223" :question/math-academy-id "q-2944"}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Logarithms Using Exponents"} {:db/id 17592186064067 :question/id #uuid "d137aa5c-f148-5a6f-bbda-0d88557f8ea9" :question/math-academy-id "e-3987" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186064192 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cc1c6931-cc04-5014-9bf6-5ebc5dc07728" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Logarithms Using Exponents"}] :question/problem "Find the value of $\log_{3}{9}$." :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite $9$ as a power of $3$ (the base of the logarithm) as follows:

$$
9 = 3^2
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\log_{3}{9} = \log_{3}(3^2)
$$

Now we can proceed as usual. The log of a power of the base equals the power itself:

$$
\log_b(b^x) = x
$$

In our case, we have $b = 3$ and $x = 2$. Therefore,

$$
\log_{3}(3^2) = 2
$$"} {:db/id 17592186064667 :question/id #uuid "efed6494-6266-5ffa-88eb-576a200cbbd2" :question/math-academy-id "q-25790"} {:db/id 17592186064707 :question/id #uuid "c7faad3f-25a6-5d96-89ca-9640b6346ec0" :step/math-academy-id 14022 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065032}} {:db/id 17592186065044 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065355 :tutorial/content "We can evaluate some logarithm expressions by using the fact that the logarithm reverses the action of the exponent.

The idea is that the log of a power of the base equals the power itself:

$$
\log_b(b^x) = x
$$

For example, in the case of

$$
\log_2 \left(2^{-1/2}\right)
$$

we have $b=2$ and

$$
x=-\dfrac 1 2
$$

Therefore,

$$
\log_2\left(2^{-1/2}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3299e585-1c90-521e-8207-847f81227d56" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2865 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "555e3d58-f4f5-5c7c-8a56-80938dcac0c2" :step/math-academy-id 15298 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065030}} {:db/id 17592186065045 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065356 :tutorial/content "When the argument of the logarithm isn't written as an exponential, we can often still evaluate the logarithm. All we need to do is rewrite the argument so that it is in the form $b^x$, where $b$ is the base of the logarithm.

For instance, to evaluate

$$
\log_2\left(8\right)
$$

we rewrite $8$ as a power of $2$ (the base of the logarithm) as follows:
$8 = 2^{3}$

Therefore, we have

$$
\log_{2}{8} = \log_{2}\left(2^{3}\right)
$$

Now we can proceed as before. The log of a power of the base equals the power itself:

$$
\log_b(b^x) = x
$$

In our case, we have $b = 2$ and $x = 3$. Therefore,

$$
\log_{2}\left(2^{3}\right) = 3
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1a5e22c2-205f-5cd6-bf98-c67977b99b73" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2866 :tutorial/title "Evaluating Logarithms Using Exponents"} :step/id #uuid "52e5cb38-4eef-573d-ba63-00b902ef60bd" :step/math-academy-id 15299 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065033}} {:db/id 17592186065046 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065357 :tutorial/content "Recall that two special cases of exponentials are

$$
n^0 =1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad n^1 =n
$$

What do these look like in logarithm form? We can use the definition of a logarithm to find out:

> $a = {n}^{x}$ is equivalent to $\log_{n}{a} = {x}$.

Using the above, we have that $n^0 =1$ is equivalent to

$$
\log_n 1 = 0
$$

Also, we have that $n^1 =n$ is equivalent to

$$
\log_n n = 1
$$

These are two special values for logarithms that are true for any base

$$
n>0, n \neq 1
$$

**Watch out!** We should always assume that the base $n$ of the logarithm does not equal $1$. Recall that

$$
\log_n{a} = x
$$

is equivalent to
$a = n^x$. If $n=1$ that transforms to
$a = 1^x$.
Now, we have the following two possibilities:

- if $a \neq 1$, we get that $a \neq 1^x$ for any real $x$, and
- if $a = 1$, we obtain that $1 = 1^x$ for all real $x$.

In both cases, the notation $\log_1{a}$ does not make much sense." :tutorial/id #uuid "e668e2ae-df5f-5d1e-919a-80f3b07c0b72" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2867 :tutorial/title "Special Values of Logarithms"} :step/id #uuid "5f6eb5ac-5827-5b3b-96ac-7f951bbe5b1f" :step/math-academy-id 15300 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065031}}] :activity/title "Evaluating Logarithms" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064462} {:db/id 17592186065044 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065355 :tutorial/content "We can evaluate some logarithm expressions by using the fact that the logarithm reverses the action of the exponent.

$f(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(z).$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,1,\pi ).$" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,1,\pi )$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(0,1,\pi )+∇f(0,1,\pi )\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z-\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(0,1,\pi )=-1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(0,1,\pi )=-1, \\ {f}_{y} & =x{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(0,1,\pi )=0, \\ {f}_{z} & =-{e}^{xy}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(0,1,\pi )=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(0,1,\pi )$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(0,1,\pi ) & =⟨{f}_{x}(0,1,\pi ),{f}_{y}(0,1,\pi ),{f}_{z}(0,1,\pi )⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(0,1,\pi )+∇f(0,1,\pi )\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z-\pi ⟩ \\  & ≈-1+⟨-1,0,0⟩\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z-\pi ⟩ \\  & ≈-1-x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186125008 :question/id #uuid "0ed320f7-bb9c-5ef9-a5ac-93165087275f" :question/math-academy-id "q-36747"} {:db/id 17592186235526 :question/id #uuid "Let $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2).$" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={e}^{y}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=2, \\ {f}_{y} & =x{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-1{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =⟨2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇\,f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+⟨2,-2⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+2(x+1)-2(y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+2x-2y.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186404953 :question/id #uuid "f0a65ec3-c24d-50c1-a1d2-f9666a246122" :question/math-academy-id "q-98554"} {:db/id 17592186404960 :question/id #uuid "ec12843c-221e-5977-accb-d9e9aa80cb79" :question/math-academy-id "q-98555"} {:db/id 17592186420930 :question/id #uuid "55146915-2d47-5b59-9386-37303589ba19" :question/math-academy-id "q-129741" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "19a5d7fe-a63b-5e32-949d-b3f2969e0db8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x,y)≈-2x-y" :db/id 17592186420919} {:answer/id #uuid "3a60a799-4271-555e-b402-ed7491785238" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x,y)≈-1-2x+y" :db/id 17592186420921} {:answer/id #uuid "9c37dd2d-538f-57a0-aa67-b6fb35e4d8ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x,y)≈2+x+2y" :db/id 17592186420923} {:answer/id #uuid "b8cdea38-23c3-571a-bf79-4dd2da2d05bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x,y)≈-x-2y" :db/id 17592186420924} {:answer/id #uuid "fe73bc79-52e6-53a8-9039-023077c29e7f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x,y)≈-1-2x-4y" :db/id 17592186420928}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186420921} :answer-field/id #uuid "71f2f20d-59aa-5f4b-b243-cfacb310155a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186420929}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)={x}^{2}{e}^{y}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,0)=1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =2x{e}^{y}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(-1,0)=-2, \\ {f}_{y} & ={x}^{2}{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(-1,0)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,0) & =⟨-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\  & ≈1+⟨-2,1⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\  & ≈1-2(x+1)+y \\  & ≈-1-2x+y.\end{aligned}

f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-2,-3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,y+3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-2,-3)=-19.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={y}^{2}\, &  & ⇒\,{f}_{x}(-2,-3)=(-3)^{2}=9, \\ {f}_{y} & =2xy &  & ⇒\,{f}_{y}(-2,-3)=2(-2)(-3)=12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-2,-3)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-2,-3) & =⟨9,12⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-2,-3)+∇\,f(-2,-3)\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+⟨9,12⟩\cdot ⟨x+2,\,y+3⟩ \\  & =-19+9(x+2)+12(y+3) \\  & =35+9x+12y.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186489249 :question/id #uuid "9d2fd7c0-6fec-5b30-98fe-3b0bf10ba9a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-65338" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124451 :knowledge-point/id #uuid
