Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)+\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $3.$ Therefore,
$\omega =3.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =3$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[(6D-9Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-(6C+9Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)]+9t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =-12\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ 6D\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-6C\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =-12\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=\frac{1}{2}$ and $D=-2.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)+\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)+\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Solutions I, II, and III match the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"."} :step/id #uuid "63616043-21be-5d80-99e6-bbe839235312"} {:db/id 17592186442744 :step/content {:db/id 17592186435716 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6c18230a-149d-58ba-93cf-40b239913f25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186435697} {:answer/id #uuid "065c1236-c8cd-5e0a-8536-ab48d1fe6aae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.5" :db/id 17592186442733}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442733} :answer-field/id #uuid "75523a18-6820-5b9b-bc7e-e9376c4fa924" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186435710}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "189994a2-e868-5656-b67a-5717b59ea689" :question/math-academy-id "q-343698" :question/problem "A particle of mass $0.5\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. {{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.5{y}^{″}=-ky+2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+2ky=4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=2k\,⟹\,k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t)$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$ Since

$$
f(t)=4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3}{2}t)=2(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)),
$$

the frequency of the external periodic force is $3.$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot {3}^{2}=\frac{9}{2}\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

$$

$$

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

$$

$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $D=0.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+ϕ)-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\frac{3}{2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

The external force is $f(t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $4.$ Therefore,
$\omega =4.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)).
$$

$$

$$

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Solutions I, II, and III match the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"."} :step/id #uuid "aa755d32-f5f0-5147-8e10-608442403c58"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186495189} :activity/id #uuid "45da9bbc-1512-5651-8f30-bc8c978f6a42" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048966 :topic/id #uuid "cfd9de67-b6d3-5aac-81ab-498c732e22a6" :topic/math-academy-id 6720} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186495178 :step/content {:db/id 17592186495094 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f1673e8-dffa-58ad-a21d-370ac4f21d2f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186494409}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494409} :answer-field/id #uuid "e18cc19c-c2dd-5d83-85f6-24d5473b0766" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186495028}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "64d62ce0-8437-5a77-8100-0fa04bf9d1d8" :question/math-academy-id "q-343690" :question/problem "A particle of mass $0.8\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. {{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.8{y}^{″}=-ky+(4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{5}{2}t)-2).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{4}y=\frac{5}{2}(2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{5}{2}t)-1).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{4}\,⟹\,k=\frac{4}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=\frac{5}{2}(2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{5}{2}t)-1)$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$ Since

$$
f(t)=\frac{5}{2}(2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{5}{2}t)-1)=\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),
$$

the frequency of the external periodic force is $5.$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{4}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{4}{5}\cdot {5}^{2}=20\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "04593abc-de35-5ea9-a146-5ea660c1a706" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495252}} {:db/id 17592186495252 :step/content {:db/id 17592186442740 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10ac45f2-8682-5e38-90a5-af6b3b0df052" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186442734} {:answer/id #uuid "720de89b-25be-516b-9df5-32bca90894e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186442735} {:answer/id #uuid "8b3b3ddc-f2b0-5960-a120-6e3182615388" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186442736} {:answer/id #uuid "90774d44-8df7-5a01-b829-eff4553b5ba9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186442737} {:answer/id #uuid "eb5401b3-3249-566f-8e5f-01020ae0590b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186442738}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442736} :answer-field/id #uuid "c3260424-876c-50ae-ac8b-7b96731c9907" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186442739}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ee642054-1d27-50a4-8f05-345ca578dfc0" :question/math-academy-id "q-343743" :question/problem "A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)+\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants." :question/worked-solution "Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $3.$ Therefore,
$\omega =3.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =3$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[9(D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9(C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)]+9t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ 9D\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9C\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=-\frac{2}{3}$ and $D=0.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t+ϕ)-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t+ϕ)-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$

Only solution II matches the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "II only"."} :step/id #uuid "c95a38fe-1860-539e-b737-8be81b3f72b1"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3210051c-3999-5418-903e-b15e38e02322" :answer/type $$
20%=\frac{20}{100}
$$

We can simplify the fraction by dividing the numerator and denominator by $10:$

$$
\frac{20}{100}=\frac{20÷10}{100÷10}=\frac{2}{10}
$$

Then, we divide the numerator and denominator by $2:$

$$
\frac{2}{10}=\frac{2÷2}{10÷2}=\frac{1}{5}
$$

Now, notice that

$$
\frac{1}{5}<\frac{2}{5}.
$$

Therefore, $20%$ is equivalent to $\frac{1}{5},$ 
which is $\text{smaller than}$ $\frac{2}{5}.$"} {:db/id 17592186147798 :question/id #uuid "8f6c9244-7a57-598c-9661-2f1767ee2033" :question/math-academy-id "q-348952"} {:db/id 17592186434387 :question/id #uuid "138791bc-5cad-58ca-ae3d-64015f9ea134" :question/math-academy-id "q-349678" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6fc398c3-ef25-52ba-8a15-a914c2acb08b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "equal to" :db/id 17592186434378} {:answer/id #uuid "cb6ea343-a5aa-5d69-b351-d0c27cab6e7f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "greater than" :db/id 17592186434382} {:answer/id #uuid "f52cda3d-118c-5960-b7d2-b5e6e6485224" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "smaller than" :db/id 17592186434383}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186434382} :answer-field/id #uuid "0b435f79-e45f-54bc-a9c1-2ebc68f39df2" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186434385} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "355f6139-1632-5fb9-a099-f60c0204143d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{17}{40}" :db/id 17592186434373} {:answer/id #uuid "43eb7fb9-45e1-5182-81e4-f59709d8a423" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16}{40}" :db/id 17592186434374} {:answer/id #uuid "4da1f349-69e6-5209-8396-1c722ffbf3d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{18}{40}" :db/id 17592186434375} {:answer/id #uuid "4e451e41-9d76-5570-9fd1-85be78bfe38d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{20}{40}" :db/id 17592186434376}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186434375} :answer-field/id #uuid "c1896846-f13a-5c11-a37a-ffc9a894ca42" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186434386}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Select the options that make the statement below true.

In the previous season, $12%$ of Lionel’s goals were scored from the penalty spot, while the decimal proportion of David’s goals scored from the penalty spot was $0.1.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. Less than half of Lionel's goals scored were from the penalty spot.

II. More than half of David's goals scored were from the penalty spot.

III. Lionel had a greater percentage of goals scored from the penalty spot compared to David.

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since 

$$
12%<50%,
$$

less than half of Lionel's goals scored were from the penalty spot.

- Statement II is false. Notice that 

$$
0.1<0.5.
$$

So, less than half of David's goals scored were from the penalty spot.

- Statement III is true. We can compare $12%$ and $0.1$ by converting the decimal into a percent. 

To do this, we multiply it by $100:$

$$
0.1\times 100=10%
$$

Since  $12%>10%,$ Lionel had a **greater** percentage of goals scored from the penalty spot compared to David.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only"."} {:db/id 17592186147802 :question/id #uuid "f2cc0d53-2a89-5a27-98eb-885f1d459e75" :question/math-academy-id "q-350257"} {:db/id 17592186434388 :question/id #uuid "16a4ed86-6ba4-5b08-b5bc-00c64da3da49" :question/math-academy-id "q-350266" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "825bb7d0-2dd7-5898-b09d-fa36c3af945c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453868} {:answer/id #uuid "b7ee75e3-c277-58e5-8016-0f292274075f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453869}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453869} :answer-field/id #uuid "27377df2-4049-5654-9b05-2bd96fc9143a" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454684} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ffa5102c-c608-5436-b9c9-a71c559e2def" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453870} {:answer/id #uuid "c3c895d9-44a3-52c0-ab7d-3d644c95fa8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453871}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453870} :answer-field/id #uuid "90d78070-dbec-5fd0-85ce-332d66270d76" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454685} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cac6f298-f93a-5381-8ee2-f655b4a4bb52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453872} {:answer/id #uuid "91b100af-367e-5f51-bd41-32339c196cd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453873}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453872} :answer-field/id #uuid "08559b28-05c3-5429-8dcc-9459d6dd6efb" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454686}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Sana and Talia are students. For the given number, the sum of the digits is

$$
3+5+8+3+2+4+◻+2=27+◻.
$$

Now, let's consider each of the given digits we can substitute into the blank.

- If we substitute $6$ into the blank, we get $35\,832\,462,$ which is divisible by $2.$ Then the sum of the digits is $27+6=33,$ which is divisible by $3,$ so the number is also divisible by $3.$ Therefore, the number is divisible by $6.$

:tutorial/content "We can find **equivalent ratios** by multiplying or dividing all numbers in a ratio by the same value. 

To demonstrate, let's consider the following ratio:

$$
2:6
$$

If we multiply *both* numbers by $5,$ for example, we get the ratio $10:30.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,2 &  & : & \,\,\, & \,\,6 &  \\ \,\,↓\times \,5 &  &  &  & \,\,↓\times \,5 &  \\ \,10 &  & : &  & \,30 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ratios $2:6$ and $10:30$ are equivalent. 

Similarly, if we take the ratio $2:6$ and divide *both* numbers by $2,$ we get $1:3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,2 &  & : & \,\,\, & \,\,6 &  \\ \,\,↓÷\,2 &  &  &  & \,\,↓÷\,2 &  \\ \,\,1 &  & : &  & \,\,3 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ratios  $2:6$ and  $1:3$ are also equivalent." :tutorial/id #uuid "cc2c9ce9-c2b0-5d68-81db-b8b0273407f0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8203 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6aa20fa4-3163-5025-84f7-a1ddd4324cd0" :step/math-academy-id 186681 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074635}} {:db/id 17592186074635 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075035 :tutorial/content "Suppose that the following two ratios are equivalent:

In this case, we need to get $12$ from ${\color{blue}{3}},$ so we multiply ${\color{blue}{3}}$ by $4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,3 &  & : & \,\,\, & \,\,5 &  \\ \,\,↓\times \,4 &  &  &  & \,\,↓\times \,4 &  \\ 12 &  & : &  & \,\boxed{\text{[math]\phantom{0}[/math]}} & \end{aligned}
$$

So, to get ![](images/50/50f3c1b8dc3b1628130d1de11abcc455fc22006f32b7486f658c8134fcc3221c.svg) from ${\color{red}{5}},$ we multiply ${\color{red}{5}}$ by $4$ as well:

"cbbdf6cb-f6ca-5deb-b060-a316432db0ee" :topic/math-academy-id 327} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065131 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065412 :tutorial/content "When we subtract a positive number from another positive number, we move towards the left on the number line. 

For example, let's consider the following subtraction problem:

$$
3 - 5
$$

To subtract $5$ from $3,$ we start at $3$ on the number line and move $5$ places to the left.

![](images/57/57ac1fe7a28ae5fefadf900d2276d499cdccf01df48b819b0aafa5347a2ec506.png)

When we do this, we land at $-2.$ Therefore, 

$$
3-5 = -2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8af27dde-6aa4-5067-84f8-9538f1acaa18" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8029 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e99d8d22-f103-5560-a608-35f0957133f4" :step/math-academy-id 188374 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065132}} {:db/id 17592186065132 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064255 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063935 :question/id #uuid "34280e7c-023c-5c7f-b22b-3f322ff97dad" :question/math-academy-id "e-12813"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6a3c970b-4086-52ef-ac0f-2b8c3d72fd51" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049429}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064527} {:db/id 17592186064570} {:db/id 17592186064629} {:db/id 17592186433314} {:db/id 17592186433317} {:db/id 17592186433318} {:db/id 17592186433319} {:db/id 17592186433320} {:db/id 17592186515582}] :knowledge-point/title "Subtracting a Positive Number From a Non-Negative Number"} :step/id #uuid "a7e8a41f-1f30-5c54-b22b-c51e7a5efd82" :step/math-academy-id 188375 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065133}} {:db/id 17592186065133 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065413 :tutorial/content "It is impractical to use number lines to subtract large numbers. 

However, a neat trick makes subtracting a positive number from a smaller positive number very easy!

As an example, let's consider the following subtraction problem:

$$
{\color{red}{37}} - {\color{blue}{68}}
$$

Since $68$ is larger than $37,$ the answer *must be negative*.

We start by solving an easier problem: subtracting the numbers *in the reverse order*. In our case, the reverse problem is

$$
{\color{blue}{68}} - {\color{red}{37}}.
$$

Next, we carry out the subtraction:

![](images/db/db192e5c1f089e3d4cc2a7b1238392e44a7ba36bff99345a997042c16ebc304f.svg)

So, we have

$$
{\color{blue}{68}} - {\color{red}{37}} = 31.
$$

However, since our answer must be negative, we need to change the sign of the answer above. 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{\color{red}{37}} - {\color{blue}{68}} = -31.
$$

However, a neat trick makes subtracting a positive number from a smaller positive number very easy!

As an example, let's consider the following subtraction problem:

$$
{\color{red}{37}} - {\color{blue}{68}}
$$

Since $68$ is larger than $37,$ the answer *must be negative*.

We start by solving an easier problem: subtracting the numbers *in the reverse order*. In our case, the reverse problem is

$$
{\color{blue}{68}} - {\color{red}{37}}.
$$

Next, we carry out the subtraction:

![](images/db/db192e5c1f089e3d4cc2a7b1238392e44a7ba36bff99345a997042c16ebc304f.svg)

So, we have

$$
{\color{blue}{68}} - {\color{red}{37}} = 31.
$$

However, since our answer must be negative, we need to change the sign of the answer above. 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{\color{red}{37}} - {\color{blue}{68}} = -31.
$$

And that's it! 

Let's use the same idea to subtract two three-digit numbers." :tutorial/id #uuid "d7dbb60e-47d5-56db-981a-145c532f7ace" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8030 :tutorial/title "Subtraction With Larger Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "12b96179-bf32-5136-bbf1-e7631a656dfb" :step/math-academy-id 188379 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065134}} {:db/id 17592186065413 :tutorial/content "It is impractical to use number lines to subtract large numbers.

The first rule says that when we multiply a negative number by a positive number, the result (**product**) is a negative number. We can picture this multiplication rule as

$$
(-)\cdot(+) = (-)or(+)\cdot(-) = (-)
$$

For instance, let's find out the value of $(-3) \cdot 10$.
Here, we have a product of a negative number $\color{red}(-3)$ and a positive one ${\color{blue}(10)}$. So the product will be negative:
$30$
Now, to compute the number that goes in the box, we multiply $3$ by $10$ without any signs:

$$
3 \cdot 10 = 30
$$

So, we get

$$
{\color{red}(-3)} \cdot {\color{blue}10} = {\color{red} -30}
$$

Note that multiplication is **commutative**, meaning it doesn't matter in what order we multiply two numbers. Commutativity means that we're allowed to swap the numbers, which gives

$$
{\color{red}(-3)} \cdot {\color{blue}10} = {\color{blue}10}\cdot {\color{red}(-3)} = {\color{red} -30}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1eb02261-90e4-51bc-a24e-dabdedaafa63" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8105 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "480bb98f-29a4-57e1-9342-972680f415f8" :step/math-academy-id 82238 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065294}} {:db/id 17592186065294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064363 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063939 :question/id #uuid "9e3473f6-80c1-5559-b29f-ac0bcb2f3a13" :question/math-academy-id "e-12967"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "75901336-1d0e-51f1-acde-d6eb784d9f82" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049429}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064550} {:db/id 17592186064576} {:db/id 17592186432267} {:db/id 17592186432268}] :knowledge-point/title "Multiplying a Positive Number by a Negative Number"} :step/id #uuid "cb9bb839-e0dc-5aca-9cc9-ae22d07a3486" :step/math-academy-id 82239 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065295}} {:db/id 17592186065295 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064364 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063940 :question/id #uuid "e4e645fe-d1cd-584c-b6a3-4e75e1170a34" :question/math-academy-id "e-12969"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9cb97145-a93a-5df3-8dbe-6777d21601c8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186051030}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064767} {:db/id 17592186064940} {:db/id 17592186064974} {:db/id 17592186424824} {:db/id 17592186432266} {:db/id 17592186515611}] :knowledge-point/title "Multiplying a Positive Number by a Negative Number With Decimals"} :step/id #uuid "b387ed41-0522-5959-a882-fcd13a445bf5" :step/math-academy-id 82242}] :activity/title "Multiplying Positive Numbers With Negative Numbers" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064401} {:db/id 17592186065293 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065415 :tutorial/content "Multiplying with negative numbers can be summed up by two simple rules.

:topic/math-academy-id 2457} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186148482 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148698 :tutorial/content "When working with fractions, percents, and decimals, we often need to decide which number is greater or smaller. Since these numbers are written in different forms, it can be difficult to compare them directly.

To make comparisons easier, we can *convert them to a common form*.

For example, let's compare the percent $48\%$ and the decimal $0.52$.

One way to do that is to convert the percent to a decimal. So, we divide the percent value by $100{:}$

$$
48 \div 100 = 0.48
$$

Thus, $48\%$ is equivalent to $0.48$.

Now, we can compare the two decimals:
$0.48 < 0.52$

Therefore, we can conclude that $48\%$ is smaller than $0.52$.

Let's see more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "e6681afa-a432-5074-a46c-204561f2cf65" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2078 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d9c7592c-10c0-5cc3-b1ff-b5b67dfe08ba" :step/math-academy-id 632742 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148483}} {:db/id 17592186148483 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147542 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147245 :question/id #uuid "7dd3b106-ac45-522a-97ea-6dc4355f0247" :question/math-academy-id "e-2317"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6be40082-db16-5983-aa43-9b6ee8f59def" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049298} {:db/id 17592186050030}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186147795} {:db/id 17592186147796}] :knowledge-point/title "Comparing a Decimal to a Percent"} :step/id #uuid "5df02fb6-3576-5996-8b1e-64978fa7b5d8" :step/math-academy-id 632743 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148484}} {:db/id 17592186148484 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147543 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147246 :question/id #uuid "22bfefb3-89b4-5d42-b305-732790c89fbd" :question/math-academy-id "e-2318"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "37060efd-560b-5d57-b108-07c202e3abcc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049640} {:db/id 17592186050478}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186147797} {:db/id 17592186147798} {:db/id 17592186434387}] :knowledge-point/title "Comparing a Percent to a Fraction"} :step/id #uuid "f6835341-5e27-57e3-ae67-a97b6df1ba75" :step/math-academy-id 632746 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148485}} {:db/id 17592186148485 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148670 :tutorial/content "Suppose Ethan and Ryan are baseball players. In the previous season, $24\%$ of Ethan’s hits were home runs, while the decimal proportion of Ryan’s hits that were home runs was $0.3$.

Let’s determine whether either Ethan or Ryan hit home runs on more than half of their total hits.

- *For Ethan*, we compare his statistic to one-half written as a percentage, $50\%$. Since
$24\% < 50\%$,
less than half of Ethan’s hits were home runs.
- *For Ryan*, we compare his statistic to one-half written as a decimal, $0.5$. Since
$0.3 < 0.5$,
less than half of Ryan’s hits were home runs.

Therefore, neither player hit home runs on more than half of their hits.

Now, let’s see more concrete examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "fbb4d977-7db5-579e-baf0-bb8e13b6c15a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14935 :tutorial/title "Comparing Decimals and Percents in Context"} :step/id #uuid "4ce04142-5c86-5b4c-a76f-55af88901484" :step/math-academy-id 632749 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148486}} {:db/id 17592186148486 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147544 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147235 :question/id #uuid "4016fd3c-d8b2-5ef2-8554-47ac5c183950" :question/math-academy-id "e-22017"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "638e604b-5416-5d3c-a61f-5be645aa255b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186147801} {:db/id 17592186147802} {:db/id 17592186434388} {:db/id 17592186515567}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements in Context"} :step/id #uuid "c0e51654-69d7-5097-b27f-71f3c28bce97" :step/math-academy-id 632750 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148487}} {:db/id 17592186148487 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148671 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose Carlos and Henry have the same number of trading cards. A total of $32 \%$ of Carlos's cards are rare cards, while

$$
\dfrac{1}{4}
$$

of Henry's cards are rare cards.

Who has more rare cards?

To answer this, we need to *compare the fraction and the percentage*:

$$
\dfrac{1}{4} \qquad\text{and}\qquad 32 \%
$$

A common method is to convert the fraction to a percentage.

First, we write

$$
\dfrac{1}{4}
$$

as an equivalent fraction with $100$ as the denominator:

$$
\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1 \times 25}{4 \times 25} = \dfrac{25}{100}
$$

Now, we can write this fraction as a percentage:

$$
\dfrac{25}{100} = 25 \%
$$

Since $25 \% < 32 \%$, we can conclude that Carlos has *more* rare cards than Carlos." :tutorial/id #uuid "4be68676-8fcc-56ce-a8ef-96b2a954a03c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14937 :tutorial/title "Comparing Fractions and Percents in Context"} :step/id #uuid "99330381-c770-5a62-a3c7-a79ba13fcd0b" :step/math-academy-id 632753 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148488}} {:db/id 17592186148488 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147545 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147247 :question/id #uuid "e6b550b1-cd66-5a70-9d11-d37733ac4c5f" :question/math-academy-id "e-2319"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9d39373d-ba41-53aa-8119-4ecf5138a50a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186147799} {:db/id 17592186147800} {:db/id 17592186424830}] :knowledge-point/title "Comparing Fractions and Percents: Word Problem"} :step/id #uuid "5102e680-a474-5349-a6c9-27bc67303b7a" :step/math-academy-id 632754}] :activity/title "Comparing Fractions, Percents, and Decimals" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186147658} {:db/id 17592186148482 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148698 :tutorial/content "When working with fractions, percents, and decimals, we often need to decide which number is greater or smaller. For example:

$$
{\color{purple}-\dfrac{1}{2}}, \quad {\color{purple}\dfrac{1}{2}}, \quad {\color{purple}\dfrac{1}{3}}, \quad {\color{purple}-\dfrac{2}{3}}, \quad {\color{purple}\dfrac{2}{3}}
$$

Every integer is also a rational number because every integer can be expressed as a ratio of two integers. For example,

$$
{\color{blue}2} = {\color{black}\dfrac{2}{1}}, \qquad {\color{red}-9} = {\color{black}\dfrac{(-9)}{\phantom{-}1}}
$$

Likewise, any mixed number is a rational number because it can be written as an improper fraction. For example,

$$
2 \, \dfrac{1}{3}
$$

is a rational number because

$$
2 \, \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2 \times 3 + 1}{3} = \dfrac{7}{3}
$$

We can now add the rational numbers to our inclusion diagram.

![](images/12/124ced6b317bdd2df4f967e6ea45e613b89d9fa136acb5edf8f7ed86fa8a4c06.png)

Notice that the integers (and therefore the natural numbers) are contained within the rational numbers." :tutorial/id #uuid "3563ca37-8d82-5742-92b2-bb3918a71477" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9071 :tutorial/title "The Rational Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "cc715ab1-8b8b-555b-bd73-97d8d33107c0" :step/math-academy-id 172688 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153007}} {:db/id 17592186153007 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152126 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151861 :question/id #uuid "471f680f-5a51-5dac-aa3c-834610690f0e" :question/math-academy-id "e-14644"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f7063140-eebe-598c-b530-3c13509d359b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152877} {:db/id 17592186152878} {:db/id 17592186424829} {:db/id 17592186433607} {:db/id 17592186433608}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Numbers as Rational"} :step/id #uuid "ba79c281-b939-528f-8605-0a6cd2aa6abd" :step/math-academy-id 172689 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153008}} {:db/id 17592186153008 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153468 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following rational number:

$$
\dfrac13
$$

We can find the decimal representation of this rational number by dividing $1$ by $3$ using long division, as follows:

| $\,\,0 \,. 3 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 3 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 3$$\:\ldots$$3$$\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{1 {\,. \,} 0 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 0 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 0}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$9$$1$$0$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$9$$1$$0$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$9$$1$$\,\ldots$ |
| --- |

Note that, in this case

- the long division process never ends, and
- the digit $3$ after the decimal point repeats *forever*.

Therefore, we have that

$$
\dfrac13 = 0.333\,333\ldots
$$

This is an example of a **repeating decimal**. A repeating decimal is a decimal where the digits after the decimal point continue forever but in a repeating pattern.

It's convenient to use the following special notation to indicate decimals that repeat indefinitely.

$$
0.\overline{3} = 0.333\,333\ldots
$$

Some decimals have two or more digits that repeat indefinitely. For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.78^(―) &= 0.78787878… \\
0.675^(―) &= 0.675675675…
\end{aligned}
$$

Some repeating decimals have non-repeating digits before the repeating part. For example:

$$
0.333\overline{67} = 0.333\,67\,67\,67\,67\ldots
$$

The key takeaway for this section is that every repeating decimal is rational! In other words, every repeating decimal can be expressed as a ratio of two integers.

For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.3^(―) &= \frac{1}{3} \\
0.78^(―) &= \frac{26}{33} \\
0.33367^(―) &= \frac{16517}{49500}
\end{aligned}
$$

In a future lesson, we'll learn how to express a repeating decimal as a fraction. $$

We can find the decimal representation of this rational number by dividing $1$ by $3$ using long division, as follows:

| $\,\,0 \,. 3 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 3 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 3$$\:\ldots$$3$$\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{1 {\,. \,} 0 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 0 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 0}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$9$$1$$0$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$9$$1$$0$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$9$$1$$\,\ldots$ |
| --- |

Note that, in this case

- the long division process never ends, and
- the digit $3$ after the decimal point repeats *forever*.

Therefore, we have that

$$
\dfrac13 = 0.333\,333\ldots
$$

This is an example of a **repeating decimal**. A repeating decimal is a decimal where the digits after the decimal point continue forever but in a repeating pattern.

It's convenient to use the following special notation to indicate decimals that repeat indefinitely.

$$
0.\overline{3} = 0.333\,333\ldots
$$

Some decimals have two or more digits that repeat indefinitely. For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.78^(―) &= 0.78787878… \\
0.675^(―) &= 0.675675675…
\end{aligned}
$$

Some repeating decimals have non-repeating digits before the repeating part. For example:

$$
0.333\overline{67} = 0.333\,67\,67\,67\,67\ldots
$$

The key takeaway for this section is that every repeating decimal is rational! In other words, every repeating decimal can be expressed as a ratio of two integers.

For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.3^(―) &= \frac{1}{3} \\
0.78^(―) &= \frac{26}{33} \\
0.33367^(―) &= \frac{16517}{49500}
\end{aligned}
$$

- $-314\,159 \times 0 = 0$
- $0\times 0 = 0$

To see *why* multiplying any number by zero always equals zero, let's take a look at the multiplication table for $5$, shown below.

$$
\begin{aligned}
5 \cdot 4 &= 20 \\
5 \cdot 3 &= 15 \\
5 \cdot 2 &= 10 \\
5 \cdot 1 &= 5 \\
5 \cdot 0 &= ◻
\end{aligned}
$$

As we go down the list, the number in blue is reduced by $5$ each time. Following this pattern, we must have

$$
\color{blue}\square = 0
$$

.

Note that, since multiplication is commutative, multiplying zero by any number (including itself) equals zero as well. Some examples are shown below.

- $0 \times 5 = 0$
- $0 \times 123 = 0$
- $0 \times -314\,159 = 0$
- $0 \times 0 = 0$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7ed778da-8d5a-5363-972b-d9435e22a0e1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3119 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "77ea407f-55c3-5258-ba3f-15c16ab12b9a" :step/math-academy-id 16956 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065090}} {:db/id 17592186065090 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064228 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064086 :question/id #uuid "078b5c64-d765-52da-9d87-56c23618c6a6" :question/math-academy-id "e-4635"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "42032d61-c2d5-5154-9a9d-d93e69d1ba53" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064769} {:db/id 17592186064923}] :knowledge-point/title "Multiplying a Number by Zero"} :step/id #uuid "32f923a1-966b-5c2d-aa49-a238ba8d46c2" :step/math-academy-id 16957 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065091}} {:db/id 17592186065091 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065363 :tutorial/content "Dividing zero by any number (other than zero) always equals zero. [{:db/id 17592186172716 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173299 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we studied some rules for determining if an integer is divisible by $2,5,10,4,$ and $8.$ In this lesson, we'll extend our understanding of divisibility rules to include $3,9,6,$ and $7.$

We have the following rule for determining if a number is divisible by $3{:}$

*A number is divisible by $3$ if the sum of its digits is divisible by $3.$*

For example, let's determine if the following number is divisible by $3{:}$

$$
312\,561
$$

If we sum the digits, we get

$$
3+1+2+5+6+1 = 18.
$$

Now, since $18$ is divisible by $3,$ we conclude that $312\,561$ is divisible by $3.$

The rule for determining if a number is divisible by $9$ is similar:

*A number is divisible by $9$ if the sum of its digits is divisible by $9.$*

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "0b0f6b89-66c8-5e63-9825-60eb62f1271f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9390 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1794b655-2bac-5203-8fdb-02da477fb69d" :step/math-academy-id 172668 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172717}} {:db/id 17592186172717 :step/content {:db/id 17592186171932 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171756 :question/id #uuid "b926f4d4-513a-5b05-8ce2-bedc39784ada" :question/math-academy-id "e-15012"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fb8fa39c-a982-569a-b2e0-833c51259711" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048145} {:db/id 17592186048967}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172310} {:db/id 17592186172602} {:db/id 17592186432788} {:db/id 17592186432792} {:db/id 17592186432793} {:db/id 17592186432794} {:db/id 17592186515522}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining if a Number Is Divisible by 3 or 9"} :step/id #uuid "b30e2ba3-941c-5d16-b861-02db07423b35" :step/math-academy-id 172669 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172718}} {:db/id 17592186172718 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173304 :tutorial/content "We have the following rule for determining if a number is divisible by $6{:}$

*A number is divisible by $6$ if it is divisible by both $2$ and $3.$*

For example, let's determine if the following number is divisible by $6{:}$

$$
353,856
$$

To check whether this number is divisible by $6,$ we need to check that it's divisible by *both* $2$ *and* $3{:}$

- Notice that the last digit of $353,85{\color{blue}{6}}$ is ${\color{blue}{6}}.$ Since ${\color{blue}{6}}$ is even, $353,856$ is divisible by $2.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

- We now check for divisibility by $3.$ The sum of the digits is

$$

$$

Since $30$ is divisible by $3,$ we have that $353,856$ is divisible by $3.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

So, since $353,856$ is divisible by *both* $2$ *and* $3,$ we conclude that it is divisible by $6.$

I. $6$

II. $7$

III. $9$" :question/worked-solution "A number is divisible by $6$ if it is divisible by both $2$ and $3.$ Remember that to determine whether a number is divisible by $3,$ we check whether the sum of the digits is divisible by $3.$

For the given number, the sum of the digits is

$$
3+5+8+3+2+4+◻+2=27+◻.
$$

Now, let's consider each of the given digits we can substitute into the blank.

- If we substitute $6$ into the blank, we get $35\,832\,462,$ which is divisible by $2.$ Then the sum of the digits is $27+6=33,$ which is divisible by $3,$ so the number is also divisible by $3.$ Therefore, the number is divisible by $6.$

- If we substitute $7$ into the blank, we get $35\,832\,472,$ which is divisible by $2.$ However, it is not divisible by $3$ because the sum of the digits is $27+7=34,$ which is not divisible by $3.$ So, the number is *not* divisible by $6$ either.

:step/math-academy-id 30450 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074872}} {:db/id 17592186074871 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074966 :tutorial/content "We can write ratios as fractions by placing the first number over the second number.

So, what ratio describes the number of rectangles to triangles below?

![](images/25/25426db008d4b246f36959f51433e0a5cebe609fc01f9539d4f45af353919261.png)

First, we count the number of rectangles. We see that there are $\color{blue}4$ rectangles.

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186055836 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055942 :tutorial/content "The **Cartesian coordinate system** (or **Cartesian plane**) is a grid that we can use to understand where certain objects lie, similar to a map. This grid looks as follows:

![](images/fd/fd702a53ff1127a2432cbdd9a3c7057a08c73ac7a086454c066fa2c96bea7974.png)

It consists of a horizontal number line called the **$x$-axis** and a vertical number line called the **$y$-axis**.

The **origin** is the location where the $x$ and $y$ axes meet and is given the symbol $O.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dacc8373-6186-517b-bba8-ec1729732e4d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1431 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5cca38c5-c625-5a28-92d3-ccdcc09f108d" :step/math-academy-id 607419 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055837}} {:db/id 17592186055837 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055943 :tutorial/content "Every location on the Cartesian plane is called a **point**. Every point is identified using an $x$**-coordinate** and a $y$**-coordinate**. Together, points are expressed using an **ordered pair** of **coordinates** $(x,y).$

For example, we can mark (or **plot**) the point $A$ with coordinates $({\color{red}{3}},{\color{blue}{2}})$ by starting from $O$ and then traveling $\color{red}3$ units towards the right, followed $\color{blue}2$ units up.

![](images/c1/c1ef61dedbbcc6eedcd125c2c62cdfbaa4d9b9a12f10181714b51c060a059fd3.png)

We say that

- the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $3$,

- the $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $2$,

- the $xy$-coordinates (or just "the coordinates") of $A$ are $(3,2).$

The letter $A$ is just a label for our point. It's usually a good idea to label points!" :tutorial/id #uuid "9e7847c5-757a-5cb8-b947-9c7d806b5dc5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1432 :tutorial/title "Coordinates and Ordered Pairs"} :step/id #uuid "b81ec1ae-2147-51bf-abd0-42837ec9335a" :step/math-academy-id 607420 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055838}} {:db/id 17592186055838 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055957 :tutorial/content "Remember that a coordinate plane is made by two number lines that meet at $0.$ Since these are number lines, we can extend both to include negative numbers.

![](images/f1/f1eeb7f3bc0ab8b39e9dc7127d76a32f1dd130d380748fedc6e11b967f3878ed.png)

We plot an ordered pair $({\color{red}x},{\color{blue}y})$ similar to before, but if the number is negative, we reverse the direction. So, starting at the origin:

- if the first number is positive, move that number of places *right* along the $\color{red}x$-axis. If its negative, move *left*.

- if the second number is positive, move that number of places *up* along the $\color{blue}y$-axis. If its negative, move *down*.

To demonstrate, let's find the coordinates of the point $Q$ above.

To find the coordinates of $Q,$ we start at the origin, move $\color{red}3$ units *left*, and then $\color{blue}2$ units *down*. 

![](images/b4/b4f58f0c1ad6dc2936ed1b24c844fa82c1b1d5ec10c80e14c6a43f6f4eaf5544.png)

Since we move left, the $\color{red}x$-coordinate is negative, and since we move down, the $\color{blue}y$-coordinate is negative.

Therefore, the coordinates of $Q$ are $({\color{red}{-3}},{\color{blue}{-2}}).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7383452c-9470-5f05-b206-dffbb84808dd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2092 :tutorial/title "Extending the Coordinate Plane to Negative Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "a86683d5-cc60-54e3-a1ca-8ddc210beec5" :step/math-academy-id 607421 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055839}} {:db/id 17592186055839 :step/content ![](images/fd/fd702a53ff1127a2432cbdd9a3c7057a08c73ac7a086454c066fa2c96bea7974.png)

It consists of a horizontal number line called the **$x$-axis** and a vertical number line called the **$y$-axis**.

This grid looks as follows:

![](images/fd/fd702a53ff1127a2432cbdd9a3c7057a08c73ac7a086454c066fa2c96bea7974.png)

It consists of a horizontal number line called the **$x$-axis** and a vertical number line called the **$y$-axis**.

Every point is identified using an $x$**-coordinate** and a $y$**-coordinate**. Together, points are expressed using an **ordered pair** of **coordinates** $(x,y).$

For example, we can mark (or **plot**) the point $A$ with coordinates $({\color{red}{3}},{\color{blue}{2}})$ by starting from $O$ and then traveling $\color{red}3$ units towards the right, followed $\color{blue}2$ units up.

![](images/c1/c1ef61dedbbcc6eedcd125c2c62cdfbaa4d9b9a12f10181714b51c060a059fd3.png)

We say that

- the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $3$,

- the $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $2$,

- the $xy$-coordinates (or just "the coordinates") of $A$ are $(3,2).$

The letter $A$ is just a label for our point. It's usually a good idea to label points!" :tutorial/id #uuid "9e7847c5-757a-5cb8-b947-9c7d806b5dc5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1432 :tutorial/title "Coordinates and Ordered Pairs"} {:db/id 17592186055838 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055957 :tutorial/content "Remember that a coordinate plane is made by two number lines that meet at $0.$ Since these are number lines, we can extend both to include negative numbers.

![](images/f1/f1eeb7f3bc0ab8b39e9dc7127d76a32f1dd130d380748fedc6e11b967f3878ed.png)

We plot an ordered pair $({\color{red}x},{\color{blue}y})$ similar to before, but if the number is negative, we reverse the direction. So, starting at the origin:

- if the first number is positive, move that number of places *right* along the $\color{red}x$-axis. If its negative, move *left*.

- if the second number is positive, move that number of places *up* along the $\color{blue}y$-axis. If its negative, move *down*.

To demonstrate, let's find the coordinates of the point $Q$ above.

To find the coordinates of $Q,$ we start at the origin, move $\color{red}3$ units *left*, and then $\color{blue}2$ units *down*. 

![](images/b4/b4f58f0c1ad6dc2936ed1b24c844fa82c1b1d5ec10c80e14c6a43f6f4eaf5544.png)

Since we move left, the $\color{red}x$-coordinate is negative, and since we move down, the $\color{blue}y$-coordinate is negative.

Therefore, the coordinates of $Q$ are $({\color{red}{-3}},{\color{blue}{-2}}).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7383452c-9470-5f05-b206-dffbb84808dd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2092 :tutorial/title "Extending the Coordinate Plane to Negative Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "a86683d5-cc60-54e3-a1ca-8ddc210beec5" :step/math-academy-id 607421 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055839}} {:db/id 17592186055957 :tutorial/content "Remember that a coordinate plane is made by two number lines that meet at $0.$ Since these are number lines, we can extend both to include negative numbers.

III. Its $y$-coordinate is $-2$" :question/worked-solution "The point $C$ is in the fourth quadrant, so statement I is false.

"$$

$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $b$ above. If the normal equation for the corresponding weighted least-squares problem $W\,A=Wb$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a & 18 \\ 18 & b\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}c \\ 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=\begin{bmatrix}{2}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {1}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 4 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}24 & 18 \\ 18 & 17\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}18 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
a+b+c=24+17+18=59.

17592186412657}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb,$ where

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,W=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=\begin{bmatrix}{2}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -4 \\ 4 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 8 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 \\ -6 & 5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}14 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & ={\begin{bmatrix}12 & -6 \\ -6 & 5\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}14 \\ -5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{12\cdot 5-(-6)\cdot (-6)}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 6 \\ 6 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}14 \\ -5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{24}\begin{bmatrix}40 \\ 24\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{3} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162351 :question/id #uuid "a22cb81e-00a5-5c3a-9983-3ce07b82cf44" :question/math-academy-id "q-137105" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8226456a-01f0-5577-ae2a-e36c51dc2d73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186159309} {:answer/id #uuid "97023f76-2165-5875-884b-00124cfc7eaf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186159310} {:answer/id #uuid "cd6021b0-6cc8-5e87-80d1-4225584902b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186159311} {:answer/id #uuid "32780e7c-aac0-5688-a09b-948445ba520b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186159312} {:answer/id #uuid "4b0c73b3-1f00-5eb0-b4a8-0954c2dec4c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186159313}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186159310} :answer-field/id #uuid "2914e011-6467-5eb9-b672-4230ceda87a3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186159308}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "$$

$$

our normal equation can be written, as follows:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}72 & -36 & 20 \\ -36 & 18 & -10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}72 & -36 & 20 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{18}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{18} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $b$ shown above. If the general solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb$ is

$$

$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 1 \\ 6 & -3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ -1 & -3 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 1 \\ 6 & -3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-22 \\ 11 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 1 \\ 6 & -3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ -4 & -12 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 1 \\ 6 & -3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-22 \\ 44 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}9 & 27 \\ 27 & 81\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-81 \\ -243\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 27 & -81 \\ 27 & 81 & -243\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}9 & 27 & -81 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-9-3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $b$ shown above. If the general solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb$ is

$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -8 & 16 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -12 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}18 & -36 \\ -36 & 72\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}27 \\ -54\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}18 & -36 & 27 \\ -36 & 72 & -54\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}18 & -36 & 27 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{3}{2}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.

$$

:topic/math-academy-id 3135} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186163036 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163308 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the least-squares problem $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where 

![](images/4d/4d538e6a37eccc1f49f34d3aa1b31a0539d50b351e6029595af1b1f7e0f2967a.svg)

Recall that the corresponding least-squares solution is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that 

$$
\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert
$$

is as small as possible.

In real-world problems, the coefficients stored in $A$ might come from sources that are not equally reliable. For example, the coefficients might be collected from population surveys with different sample sizes. As a result, we might want to assign a greater "weight" to the more reliable data.

For example, suppose we require the weight of the coefficients in the first row to be twice the weights of the other rows. Then, we can re-state our problem by saying that, for the matrix of weights $W,$ given by

![](images/72/7268fdd7c8701a9cf780342d6eab11015d7764694d17c28a2fae2336db267223.svg)

we wish to find vectors ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that 

$$
\Vert  W (A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}) \Vert
$$

is as small as possible.

Therefore, instead of solving $A\mathbf x = \mathbf{b},$ we now need to solve the least-squares problem 

$$
W\!A\mathbf x = W\mathbf{b}.
$$

To get the normal equation corresponding to this least-squares problem, we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\!A)^T{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

![](images/0c/0c7459270d9d27c40bdf5b0e6dc7eb0c7e17951541b77936804a9057f488c13f.svg)

the normal equation can be written as follows:

$$

$$

solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the least-squares problem $A\mathbf x=\mathbf{b}$ is unique, then $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ lies in $\textrm{Col}(A).$ Furthermore, $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the vector in $\textrm{Col}(A)$ that's closest to $\mathbf b.$ 

In terms of vector spaces, the vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$ Therefore, the error vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A).$

![](images/3a/3a1c79036954f0e04212892b7e3d79c75f8cd7b81d7785441f090f89a4eb6faf.png)

A similar property holds for weighted least-squares solutions:

*If the solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the least-squares problem $W\!A\mathbf x=W\mathbf{b}$ is unique, then
$A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A)$ with respect to the weighted dot product defined as 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 x_i y_i,
$$

 
where the $w_i$'s are the weights from the main diagonal of the weight matrix $W.$* 

We previously considered the weighted least-squares problem $W\!Ax=W\mathbf{b},$ where

![](images/d4/d44c48deb0864fb8fd6aa92ce8af408b600de8abf2039a3f3cd7397fabc7d9fe.svg)

It's easy to show (using the usual techniques) that the unique weighted least-squares solution is given by 

![](images/db/db8f62fcb085d8c1fcfc22bb53cb8f22bd9a65b211e5fd5d4017e30bf9bdb4c7.svg)

Computing our error vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}ε & =A\hat{x}-b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 4 \\ 14\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $\mathbf a_1$ and $\mathbf a_2$ denote the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$ 
![](images/3f/3fbafcf3f9d80d2d54089647b2f0239662dcbe56c9ba68539e2303ce752d28ee.svg)

Notice that the error vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ is *not* orthogonal to the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$

- Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{1} & =⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}⟩ \\  & =(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\  & =-3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{2} & =⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}⟩ \\  & =(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\  & =3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

However, if we check the orthogonality with respect to the *weighted* dot product 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 x_i y_i = 4x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 + x_3y_3,
\quad
$$

 

we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{⟨ε,{a}_{1}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}⟩}_{W} \\  & =4(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\  & =0\,✓ \\ {⟨ε,{a}_{2}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}⟩}_{W} \\  & =4(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A)$ with respect to the weighted dot product. We can write this as

$$
A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \perp_W \textrm{Col}(A).
$$

In terms of vector spaces, the vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the orthogonal projection with respect to $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W$ of the vector $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$ 

Furthermore, the weighted least-squares problem with weight matrix $W$ is equivalent to finding a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

$$
\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert_W
$$

\begin{aligned}ε & =A\hat{x}-b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 4 \\ 14\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $\mathbf a_1$ and $\mathbf a_2$ denote the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$ 
![](images/3f/3fbafcf3f9d80d2d54089647b2f0239662dcbe56c9ba68539e2303ce752d28ee.svg)

Notice that the error vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ is *not* orthogonal to the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$

- Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{1} & =⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}⟩ \\  & =(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\  & =-3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{2} & =⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}⟩ \\  & =(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\  & =3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

However, if we check the orthogonality with respect to the *weighted* dot product 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 x_i y_i = 4x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 + x_3y_3,
\quad
$$

 

we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{⟨ε,{a}_{1}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}⟩}_{W} \\  & =4(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\  & =0\,✓ \\ {⟨ε,{a}_{2}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}⟩}_{W} \\  & =4(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A)$ with respect to the weighted dot product. We can write this as

$$
A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \perp_W \textrm{Col}(A).
$$

In terms of vector spaces, the vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the orthogonal projection with respect to $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W$ of the vector $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$ 

Furthermore, the weighted least-squares problem with weight matrix $W$ is equivalent to finding a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

$$
\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert_W
$$

$$

$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -8 & 16 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -12 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}18 & -36 \\ -36 & 72\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}27 \\ -54\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}18 & -36 & 27 \\ -36 & 72 & -54\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}18 & -36 & 27 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{3}{2}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$
a+\frac{b}{c}=2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+\frac{2}{1}=5.

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix},
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -16 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -10\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & ={\begin{bmatrix}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9\cdot 8-(-2)\cdot (-2)}\begin{bmatrix}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{68}\begin{bmatrix}68 \\ -68\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d99942ec-6a5c-5573-82e8-6cbe4cc7bec4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186483475}} {:db/id 17592186483470 :step/content {:db/id 17592186278195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1837262d-ff49-5dc0-83dc-18a2a52a47d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186275702} {:answer/id #uuid "83ad3cee-ea0e-56c1-b1e1-0033f7ef2b3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-17" :db/id 17592186276660} {:answer/id #uuid "a6db5086-e388-525f-b82e-43ab2607f8e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186276982} {:answer/id #uuid "da92de70-9727-5c4f-a7b9-538c8d5065dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186277394} {:answer/id #uuid "ddd8000e-3029-5f03-9736-b53484ed1a2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{17}" :db/id 17592186277423}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186277394} :answer-field/id #uuid "ebadb5d8-fe72-566c-b39f-5c8e9dc439a5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186278139}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "36a6e17d-f83c-53ad-b495-79ac2ba0a0eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-158458" :question/problem "$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {1}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix},
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 1 \\ -6 & -4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 1 \\ -6 & -4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 1 \\ -6 & -4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 4 & -8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 1 \\ -6 & -4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}17 & -34 \\ -34 & 68\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & -34 & 3 \\ -34 & 68 & -6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}17 & -34 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{3}{17}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{17}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{17} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
17a+\frac{b}{c}=17(\frac{3}{17})+\frac{2}{1}=5.

$$

$$
